name: pov_and_narration
description: Who tells it and from how far away: point-of-view types, the psychic-distance ladder, tense strategy, speech and thought representation, narrator reliability, voice textures, nonfiction narration modes, and temporal manipulation.

point_of_view_types.name: first-person protagonist
point_of_view_types.definition: The central character narrates their own story in the first person, limited to what that character knows, saw, and understood.
point_of_view_types.example: I signed the statement on a Tuesday and spent the next nine years explaining why.
point_of_view_types.effect: Maximum intimacy and maximum limitation; every fact arrives already colored by the teller's interest in it.
point_of_view_types.caution: The narrator cannot report their own face, and cannot know what happened in rooms they were not in without a stated source.

point_of_view_types.name: first-person witness
point_of_view_types.definition: A minor or peripheral character narrates someone else's story from the edge of it.
point_of_view_types.example: I only worked the front desk, but I signed for every envelope that came into that building, and I remember which ones he opened himself.
point_of_view_types.effect: Preserves the protagonist's mystery while keeping the intimacy of a human teller; the narrator's limited access is the plot's engine.
point_of_view_types.caution: The witness needs a reason to be present at every crucial scene, or the seams show.

point_of_view_types.name: first-person retrospective
point_of_view_types.definition: A first-person narrator telling events from a later vantage, so the narrating self knows more than the experiencing self.
point_of_view_types.example: I thought the meeting was routine. It is worth saying now that I had been told twice, in writing, that it was not.
point_of_view_types.effect: Creates a running double perspective — innocence in the scene, judgment in the telling — and licenses foreshadowing.
point_of_view_types.caution: Decide how much the narrating self reveals early; unearned hindsight kills suspense.

point_of_view_types.name: first-person immediate
point_of_view_types.definition: First-person narration with no retrospective gap, the teller apparently reporting as events occur.
point_of_view_types.example: I am standing in the file room with the lights off and someone is coming down the hall.
point_of_view_types.effect: Urgency and total uncertainty about outcome; the narrator cannot know how it ends.
point_of_view_types.caution: Sustained over a novel it strains plausibility — nobody narrates while running.

point_of_view_types.name: first-person plural
point_of_view_types.definition: A 'we' narrator speaking for a group, town, generation, or institution.
point_of_view_types.example: We had all seen the letter before the meeting, and none of us said so at the meeting.
point_of_view_types.effect: Renders collective knowledge, complicity, and gossip; individual identity dissolves into consensus.
point_of_view_types.register: literary fiction; also the 'we' of some cultural criticism
point_of_view_types.caution: The reader will eventually ask who 'we' excludes — answer it deliberately.

point_of_view_types.name: second person
point_of_view_types.definition: Narration addressed to 'you', where 'you' is the story's protagonist.
point_of_view_types.example: You take the stairs because the elevator has a camera in it, and you tell yourself that is not why.
point_of_view_types.effect: Implicates the reader in the character's choices; produces intimacy and unease at once.
point_of_view_types.caution: Sustains for a story more easily than a novel; readers resist being told what they did.

point_of_view_types.name: second-person as disguised first
point_of_view_types.definition: Second-person narration in which 'you' is transparently the narrator addressing their own past self.
point_of_view_types.example: You were twenty-six and you believed that a paper trail would protect you.
point_of_view_types.effect: Gives self-accusation a form; distance and confession in the same pronoun.

point_of_view_types.name: third-person limited
point_of_view_types.definition: Third-person narration restricted to the perceptions, knowledge, and interiority of a single character.
point_of_view_types.example: She read the second paragraph twice. Nothing in it explained the date, and she could not think of anyone she could ask.
point_of_view_types.effect: Combines the intimacy of first person with the flexibility of third; the default mode of modern commercial and literary fiction.
point_of_view_types.caution: Every sensation reported must be available to the viewpoint character.

point_of_view_types.name: close third person
point_of_view_types.definition: Third-person limited pushed to minimal distance, the narration taking on the viewpoint character's diction, judgments, and rhythms.
point_of_view_types.example: The meeting was, in her professional opinion, a complete waste of a Thursday, and she had brought nothing to write on.
point_of_view_types.effect: The character's voice colors the narration without quotation marks; the natural home of free indirect discourse.
point_of_view_types.caution: The narrator's vocabulary must stay inside the character's; a word she would not know breaks the spell.

point_of_view_types.name: rotating third-person limited
point_of_view_types.definition: Third-person limited that changes viewpoint character at chapter or section breaks, one per unit.
point_of_view_types.example: Chapter four belongs to the examiner; chapter five reopens the same afternoon from the deputy's desk.
point_of_view_types.effect: Lets the reader hold knowledge no single character holds, producing dramatic irony without an omniscient narrator.
point_of_view_types.caution: Establish the rotation early and keep the units clean; unsignaled switches read as head-hopping.

point_of_view_types.name: third-person objective
point_of_view_types.definition: Third-person narration reporting only observable action and speech, with no access to any character's interiority.
point_of_view_types.example: He put the folder on the desk, sat down, and did not open it. Twice he looked at the door.
point_of_view_types.effect: Forces the reader to infer inner life from behavior; produces a cold, evidentiary surface.
point_of_view_types.caution: Sustained over long stretches it can leave readers unattached; pair it with high-stakes action.

point_of_view_types.name: third-person omniscient
point_of_view_types.definition: A narrator with unrestricted access to any character's mind and to facts no character knows.
point_of_view_types.example: Neither of them knew that the third copy had been filed in the wrong year, and would stay there until a clerk retired.
point_of_view_types.effect: Allows scope, irony, and information the characters lack; the voice can address time spans and populations.
point_of_view_types.register: classic and contemporary literary fiction, popular history
point_of_view_types.caution: Omniscience is a voice, not a license; without a consistent narrating personality it reads as sloppy limited third.

point_of_view_types.name: editorial omniscience
point_of_view_types.definition: Omniscient narration in which the narrator openly comments, generalizes, and passes judgment on the story.
point_of_view_types.example: It is worth pausing here to note how ordinary this all looked to the people doing it.
point_of_view_types.effect: Establishes the narrator as a thinking presence with a moral position; the reader is being talked to, not just told.
point_of_view_types.register: nineteenth-century novel, narrative nonfiction, long-form journalism
point_of_view_types.caution: The intrusions must be worth the interruption; unearned generalization reads as lecturing.

point_of_view_types.name: neutral omniscience
point_of_view_types.definition: Omniscient narration without editorial comment: the narrator moves freely among minds and facts but does not judge.
point_of_view_types.example: The examiner believed the reclassification was deliberate. The deputy believed it was an accounting error. Both filed reports that week.
point_of_view_types.effect: Breadth without a visible narrator; the reader draws the conclusions.
point_of_view_types.caution: Neutrality is itself a stance — juxtaposition can judge more sharply than commentary.

point_of_view_types.name: selective omniscience
point_of_view_types.definition: Omniscient narration that chooses to enter only one mind, holding the others closed while retaining the power to open them.
point_of_view_types.example: What the deputy thought that afternoon is not on record and will not be guessed at here; the examiner's notebook survives.
point_of_view_types.effect: The withheld access becomes meaningful — the narrator's restraint is a technique, not a limitation.

point_of_view_types.name: peripheral third person
point_of_view_types.definition: Third-person limited attached to an observer rather than the protagonist.
point_of_view_types.example: The clerk watched them come out of the conference room one at a time and could not read a single face.
point_of_view_types.effect: Keeps the protagonist opaque while retaining a human filter; the third-person cousin of the witness narrator.

point_of_view_types.name: epistolary point of view
point_of_view_types.definition: The story is told through documents — letters, emails, depositions, reports — each with its own writer and audience.
point_of_view_types.example: Memorandum, March 14. Per your request, attached is the schedule you have now asked for three times.
point_of_view_types.effect: Every document has an agenda, so unreliability is built into the form; readers assemble the truth from what nobody says outright.
point_of_view_types.caution: Each document must be plausible as a document, including its tedium; the plot has to survive that.

point_of_view_types.name: frame narrator
point_of_view_types.definition: A narrator who introduces and closes another narrator's story, standing between the reader and the inner tale.
point_of_view_types.example: I would not have believed any of it if the examiner had not shown me the notebook, which is how this account begins.
point_of_view_types.effect: Vouches for or distances the inner story, and lets the frame comment on the telling.
point_of_view_types.caution: Readers forget the frame if it does not return; plant a reminder near the middle.

point_of_view_types.name: nested narration
point_of_view_types.definition: A story containing a narrator who contains another narrator, two or more levels deep.
point_of_view_types.example: The deputy told me what the clerk had told him about the night the files were moved, and I am giving both versions here.
point_of_view_types.effect: Each level attenuates reliability; the reader is made aware of transmission as a process.
point_of_view_types.caution: Two levels are manageable; three need explicit signposting.

point_of_view_types.name: head-hopping
point_of_view_types.definition: Unsignaled shifts of viewpoint between characters within a single scene.
point_of_view_types.example: Faulty: 'She wondered whether he suspected. He did, and was surprised she had to ask.' — two minds in two sentences with no break.
point_of_view_types.effect: Named as a failure mode: the reader loses the anchor and stops investing in any single consciousness.
point_of_view_types.caution: Distinguish from true omniscience, which has a governing narrator's voice; head-hopping has none.

point_of_view_types.name: point-of-view break
point_of_view_types.definition: A deliberate, marked shift of viewpoint at a section or chapter boundary.
point_of_view_types.example: A line of white space, then: 'Across the square, the deputy was writing the same afternoon down differently.'
point_of_view_types.effect: Resets the reader's alignment cleanly and can reveal how wrong the previous viewpoint was.

point_of_view_types.name: reflector character
point_of_view_types.definition: A viewpoint character used chiefly as a lens on others, whose own arc is secondary to what they let the reader see.
point_of_view_types.example: The junior auditor is in every scene because she is the only person both sides still talk to.
point_of_view_types.effect: Solves access problems: the reflector goes where the story needs a witness.
point_of_view_types.caution: A reflector with no stake of their own eventually bores the reader.

psychic_distance_ladder.name: psychic distance level 1 — long shot
psychic_distance_ladder.definition: The greatest narrative distance: the narrator reports from outside, in the register of history or setting, with no access to any mind.
psychic_distance_ladder.example: It was the spring of 1978, and a man in a gray coat was crossing the courthouse square.
psychic_distance_ladder.effect: Establishes time, place, and scale before any consciousness is entered; the standard opening altitude.
psychic_distance_ladder.caution: Held too long, the reader has nobody to stand with.

psychic_distance_ladder.name: psychic distance level 2 — named subject
psychic_distance_ladder.definition: The narrator names the character and reports general facts about him from outside, in the narrator's diction.
psychic_distance_ladder.example: Raymond Teale had never much cared for county buildings.
psychic_distance_ladder.effect: Introduces a person as a subject of description; still the narrator's language, not his.

psychic_distance_ladder.name: psychic distance level 3 — inner report
psychic_distance_ladder.definition: The narrator reports the character's inner state plainly, in ordinary prose, from just outside him.
psychic_distance_ladder.effect: First access to interiority; efficient, unfiltered, and still narrated rather than felt.

psychic_distance_ladder.name: psychic distance level 4 — the character's idiom
psychic_distance_ladder.definition: The narration takes on the character's own vocabulary and judgment while remaining in third person and past tense.
psychic_distance_ladder.example: God, that smell — floor wax and old paper and forty years of other people's bad news.
psychic_distance_ladder.effect: The reader is inside the character's evaluation of the world; the operating range of free indirect discourse.
psychic_distance_ladder.caution: Any word the character would not use snaps the reader out.

psychic_distance_ladder.name: psychic distance level 5 — inside the sensorium
psychic_distance_ladder.definition: The closest distance: fragmentary, associative, the raw texture of perception before it has been organized into sentences.
psychic_distance_ladder.example: Wax. Paper. Somebody crying two doors down. Keep walking, keep walking.
psychic_distance_ladder.effect: Total immersion; syntax itself becomes the character's mental state.
psychic_distance_ladder.caution: Unreadable at length; used in bursts at moments of maximum pressure.

psychic_distance_ladder.name: distance modulation
psychic_distance_ladder.definition: Deliberately moving up and down the ladder within a scene rather than fixing one altitude.
psychic_distance_ladder.example: Open at level 2 to place him, drop to 4 as the meeting turns, close the section back at 1 with the square emptying.
psychic_distance_ladder.effect: Controls intimacy like a camera controls focal length; the primary tool for pacing emotional intensity.

psychic_distance_ladder.name: zoom-in transition
psychic_distance_ladder.definition: A move from greater to lesser distance across consecutive sentences.
psychic_distance_ladder.example: The building had been condemned twice. Ray had signed one of the notices. He could not remember which.
psychic_distance_ladder.effect: Draws the reader from context into consciousness; the standard way to begin a scene.
psychic_distance_ladder.caution: Skipping levels — 1 straight to 5 — reads as a lurch unless the jolt is the point.

psychic_distance_ladder.name: zoom-out transition
psychic_distance_ladder.definition: A move from lesser to greater distance, usually to end a scene or pass time.
psychic_distance_ladder.example: He could not remember which. Outside, the square filled and emptied twice before he came back down the steps.
psychic_distance_ladder.effect: Releases the reader from the character and hands time back to the narrator.

psychic_distance_ladder.name: distance whiplash
psychic_distance_ladder.definition: An abrupt, unmotivated jump between distances that disorients rather than moves the reader.
psychic_distance_ladder.example: Faulty: a paragraph of raw sensory fragments followed without break by 'The county had been settled in 1841 by Scottish sheep farmers.'
psychic_distance_ladder.effect: Named as a failure mode: the reader experiences a change of narrator rather than a change of focus.
psychic_distance_ladder.caution: Fix by adding an intermediate sentence at the level between, or by breaking the section.

tense_strategies.name: past-tense narration
tense_strategies.definition: Narration in the simple past, the default English storytelling tense.
tense_strategies.example: She opened the binder and found the March pages missing.
tense_strategies.effect: Invisible; readers stop registering it, which leaves attention for everything else.

tense_strategies.name: present-tense narration
tense_strategies.definition: Sustained narration in the simple present, as if events unfold at the moment of reading.
tense_strategies.example: She opens the binder. The March pages are gone.
tense_strategies.effect: Immediacy and restricted foreknowledge; the narrator cannot easily comment from the future.
tense_strategies.caution: Loses its charge over long stretches, and makes ordinary flashback machinery awkward.

tense_strategies.name: historical present
tense_strategies.definition: Present-tense narration of events known to be past, used for vividness within an otherwise past-tense account.
tense_strategies.example: It is the middle of March, and the deputy is standing in a records room with a box he cannot explain.
tense_strategies.effect: Pulls a past scene into the foreground; standard in oral storytelling and popular history.
tense_strategies.caution: Switching in and out of it repeatedly makes chronology hard to hold.

tense_strategies.name: future-tense narration
tense_strategies.definition: Narration cast in the future, projecting events that have not occurred.
tense_strategies.example: You will find the binder in the second drawer, and you will decide not to mention it.
tense_strategies.effect: Prophetic or instructional; strongly marked and inherently unstable.
tense_strategies.caution: Rarely sustainable past a few pages; use for framing sections.

tense_strategies.name: future-in-past
tense_strategies.definition: Use of 'would' to narrate what was still to come from the vantage of a past moment.
tense_strategies.example: It would be four years before anyone opened the box again.
tense_strategies.effect: Compresses time and signals hindsight; the workhorse of retrospective narration.
tense_strategies.caution: Each use spends a little suspense; count them.

tense_strategies.name: past perfect for flashback
tense_strategies.definition: Use of 'had' plus past participle to mark events prior to the narrative's main past timeline.
tense_strategies.example: She had asked for the schedule twice that winter, and both times had been sent a summary.
tense_strategies.effect: Locates events unambiguously before the main action.
tense_strategies.caution: Heavy in quantity; readers tire of a page of 'had'.

tense_strategies.name: past-perfect fade
tense_strategies.definition: Entering a flashback with two or three past-perfect verbs, then shifting to simple past for the body of it, and back to past perfect on the way out.
tense_strategies.pattern: had + participle (×2) → simple past (body) → had + participle (exit)
tense_strategies.example: She had driven out there once before. The road was gravel for the last mile, and the gate was open. She had not gone in.
tense_strategies.effect: Gets the reader into the earlier time and then out of the grammatical weight of it.
tense_strategies.register: standard technique in all past-tense narrative

tense_strategies.name: habitual past with 'would'
tense_strategies.definition: Narration of repeated past action using 'would' plus base verb.
tense_strategies.example: Every Friday he would carry the week's filings down to the annex and leave them on the cart.
tense_strategies.effect: Renders routine rather than event; establishes a life before the story disturbs it.
tense_strategies.caution: 'Would' also means future-in-past; keep the two uses separated by context.

tense_strategies.name: habitual past with 'used to'
tense_strategies.definition: Past habitual marked by 'used to', which additionally implies the habit has ended.
tense_strategies.example: The annex used to keep everything for seven years.
tense_strategies.effect: States the routine and its discontinuation in one clause; inherently elegiac.

tense_strategies.name: gnomic present
tense_strategies.definition: Present tense used for general truths and standing conditions inside a past-tense narrative.
tense_strategies.example: She filed it in the wrong year, which is how most records are lost.
tense_strategies.effect: Steps briefly out of the story to assert something that remains true; the essayist's move inside narrative.
tense_strategies.register: narrative nonfiction and editorially omniscient fiction
tense_strategies.caution: Every gnomic sentence is a claim; it must survive being read as one.

tense_strategies.name: present-tense frame with past narrative
tense_strategies.definition: A present-tense frame — the narrator now, at a desk, in a room — surrounding a past-tense account.
tense_strategies.example: The notebook is in front of me as I write this. In 1978 it was in a coat pocket, and the coat was in a courthouse.
tense_strategies.effect: Separates the act of telling from the events told, and lets the narrator's present state matter.

tense_strategies.name: tense shift as scene break
tense_strategies.definition: Using a change of tense, rather than white space or a header, to mark a shift between timelines.
tense_strategies.example: Past tense carries 1978; every section set in the present-day investigation runs in present tense.
tense_strategies.effect: Orients the reader instantly and without furniture, once the convention is established.
tense_strategies.caution: Establish it in the first two occurrences or readers will read the change as an error.

tense_strategies.name: present perfect for continuing relevance
tense_strategies.definition: Use of 'has/have' plus participle to mark past events whose consequences persist at the time of narration.
tense_strategies.example: No one has ever explained the March entries.
tense_strategies.effect: Connects past to narrative present; the natural tense of unresolved matters.

tense_strategies.name: progressive for duration
tense_strategies.definition: Use of the progressive aspect to hold an action open across other events.
tense_strategies.example: While the committee was still arguing about the agenda, the boxes were going out the loading dock.
tense_strategies.effect: Establishes simultaneity and makes one action the background of another.

tense_strategies.name: conditional narration
tense_strategies.definition: Narration in conditional or subjunctive mood, describing what would have happened or might have.
tense_strategies.example: Had anyone matched the two dates that spring, the whole thing would have ended in a week.
tense_strategies.effect: Narrates the road not taken; produces regret, irony, or suspense without inventing events.
tense_strategies.caution: Counterfactuals in nonfiction need evidence for their premises, not just their plausibility.

tense_strategies.name: mixed-tense braid
tense_strategies.definition: Two or more timelines carried simultaneously in different tenses across alternating sections.
tense_strategies.example: Present tense for the week of the hearing, past tense for the decade that produced it, alternating by chapter.
tense_strategies.effect: Lets the reader hold cause and consequence at once; the standard shape of investigative narrative nonfiction.
tense_strategies.caution: Needs a rigid, visible rule; readers will not tolerate ambiguity about which timeline they are in.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: direct speech
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: A character's words reproduced verbatim in quotation marks with a reporting clause.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: "I signed what they put in front of me," she said.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Maximum fidelity and dramatic presence; the reader hears the character rather than the narrator.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: free direct speech
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: Quoted speech with the reporting clause, the quotation marks, or both removed.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: I signed what they put in front of me. What else was there to do.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Removes the narrator from between reader and speaker; the page becomes voice.
speech_and_thought_representation.caution: Without tags, keep speakers distinguishable by diction, or readers will lose the thread.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: indirect speech
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: A character's words reported in the narrator's grammar, with tense and deixis shifted.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: She said that she had signed whatever they put in front of her.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Compresses speech and subordinates it to narration; useful for moving through talk quickly.
speech_and_thought_representation.caution: Loses the speaker's idiom entirely, which is sometimes the whole point of the line.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: free indirect speech
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: Speech reported without a reporting clause but with the narrator's third-person and past-tense grammar, retaining the speaker's idiom.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: She had signed what they put in front of her. What else was anybody supposed to do.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Blends the narrator's voice with the character's so the two cannot be cleanly separated.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: narrative report of a speech act
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: Narration that names the kind of speech act performed without giving its words.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: She explained the March entries twice and then refused to explain them again.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Maximum compression; keeps the narrator in charge of pace and summary.
speech_and_thought_representation.caution: A whole scene reported this way tells rather than shows; use it to skip what does not need hearing.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: summarized dialogue
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: A stretch of conversation compressed into narration, sometimes with one quoted line preserved for texture.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: They went through it for an hour — the dates, the signatures, whose initials were on the cover — and got nowhere. "Then somebody's lying," she said, and they started again.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Skips procedural talk while keeping one line at full volume.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: direct thought
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: A character's thought reproduced verbatim with a reporting clause, sometimes in italics or quotation marks.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: This is the last time I sign anything, she thought.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Presents the thought as a formed sentence in the character's head; explicit but slightly artificial.
speech_and_thought_representation.caution: People rarely think in complete sentences; overuse makes characters sound like they are dictating.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: free direct thought
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: Quoted thought with tags and typographic marks removed, running inside the narration.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: She closed the binder. Last time. The last time I sign anything.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: The reader falls into the character's mind without a signal; the boundary of narration dissolves.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: indirect thought
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: A thought reported in the narrator's grammar with an explicit mental-verb clause.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: She thought that she would never sign anything again.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Keeps a clear narrator between reader and mind; useful for cool, distanced interiority.
speech_and_thought_representation.caution: The filter verbs ('she thought', 'she felt', 'she realized') accumulate; cutting them is the single most common close-third revision.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: free indirect thought
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: Thought rendered in the narrator's tense and person but the character's idiom, without a mental-verb tag.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: She closed the binder. Never again — not a form, not a card, not a birthday cheque.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: The purest form of free indirect discourse; interiority with no visible seam.
speech_and_thought_representation.caution: Requires stable close third; from a distant narrator it reads as an unattributed opinion.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: free indirect discourse
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: The general technique in which a character's speech or thought is rendered in the narrator's third person and past tense while keeping the character's diction, judgments, and deictic anchors.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: Distant: 'She was annoyed by the delay.' Free indirect: 'Another hour of this. They would keep her here until the parking ran out, and then they would be sorry.'
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Lets narration carry a character's perspective without quotation, which is why it can be ironic, sympathetic, and unreliable at once.
speech_and_thought_representation.register: the central technique of the modern novel
speech_and_thought_representation.caution: It is also the standard device of unreliability; readers may take the character's judgment as the book's unless the frame corrects it.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: psycho-narration
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: The narrator's own account of a character's consciousness, in the narrator's language, including material the character could not articulate.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: She would not have called it fear, and did not have a word for the thing that made her check the parking lot twice.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Reaches parts of a mind the character cannot report; the narrator's advantage over first person.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: interior monologue
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: Sustained rendering of a character's thought as continuous first-person present-tense language.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: Second drawer. Not there. Second drawer of the other cabinet, then, and if it is not there either I say nothing at all.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Puts the reader in the flow of thinking rather than its summary.
speech_and_thought_representation.caution: Requires a reason to be this close; without pressure it reads as inventory.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: stream of consciousness
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: Narration imitating the associative, non-sequential movement of a mind, often with disrupted syntax and no filtering.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: Wax and paper and the woman crying two doors down and Ray at the top of the stairs with the folder that was not his folder and the light going.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Renders mental process rather than mental content; syntax carries the state.
speech_and_thought_representation.caution: Distinguish from interior monologue: this one abandons the sentence, not just the tag.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: soliloquy
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: A character speaking at length, alone or effectively alone, articulating thought as speech.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: Alone in the file room, he said it out loud twice, as though hearing it would make it a decision.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Externalizes interiority; borrowed from drama and useful when a character needs to be heard, not read.
speech_and_thought_representation.caution: In prose it needs a plausible occasion for speaking aloud.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: unattributed dialogue
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: An exchange run without speech tags, speakers distinguished by alternation and voice alone.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: "You signed it." "I signed a lot of things." "You signed this one twice."
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Accelerates an exchange to its bare rhythm; the reader hears rather than watches.
speech_and_thought_representation.caution: Limit to short exchanges between two clearly distinct speakers, and re-anchor before the reader can lose count.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: action beat as attribution
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: Replacing a speech tag with a line of the speaker's physical action in the same paragraph.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: "That is not my signature." She put the page down and did not pick it up again.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Attributes, paces, and characterizes at once, without 'said' repetition.
speech_and_thought_representation.caution: Every line beated becomes choreography; alternate with bare 'said'.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: slipped quotation
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: A short quoted phrase embedded inside a narrated sentence, the rest of the utterance reported.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: He said the entries were "an internal matter" and that he had said so already.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Preserves the telling phrase while summarizing the rest; standard practice in journalism.
speech_and_thought_representation.caution: The quoted fragment must be exact; the temptation to smooth it is the temptation to misquote.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: reported speech at second hand
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: Speech reported by one character as having been said by another, two removes from the reader.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: The deputy told me the clerk had said the boxes were moved on a Sunday.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Builds in doubt: every layer is a place the account could have changed.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: dialect rendering
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: Representation of a speaker's regional or social variety through word choice, grammar, and rhythm.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: "They never did tell us the plant was closing, and we'd been asking since the spring."
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Places a speaker socially and geographically with no narratorial comment.
speech_and_thought_representation.caution: Do it through syntax and idiom, not respelling; phonetic 'eye dialect' patronizes the speaker and slows the reader.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: thought in italics
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: Typographic convention marking direct thought without tags.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: She looked at the second signature. *Not mine.*
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Signals interiority unmistakably at a glance.
speech_and_thought_representation.caution: A crutch in close third, where free indirect thought does the same work without the typography; also lost in some ebook conversions.

speech_and_thought_representation.name: narrative report of a thought act
speech_and_thought_representation.definition: Narration naming that a character thought, decided, or realized something, without rendering the thought.
speech_and_thought_representation.example: She spent the drive home deciding what she was going to do about it.
speech_and_thought_representation.effect: Skims over interiority to keep pace; the thought's content is withheld or deferred.
speech_and_thought_representation.caution: Deferring a decision this way is a promise; pay it off or the reader feels cheated.

narrator_reliability_types.name: reliable narrator
narrator_reliability_types.definition: A narrator whose reports, readings, and evaluations the text gives the reader no reason to discount.
narrator_reliability_types.example: The examiner's account of the meeting matches the minutes, the deputy's letter, and everything the narrative later confirms.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: Lets the reader spend attention on the story rather than on the telling.
narrator_reliability_types.caution: Reliability is a construction, not a default; it is established by corroboration inside the text.

narrator_reliability_types.name: unreliable narrator
narrator_reliability_types.definition: A narrator whose account the reader has cause to correct, whether through deception, limitation, or self-deception.
narrator_reliability_types.example: He tells us he barely knew the deputy, then describes the man's handwriting, his coffee order, and the shape of his signature.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: Creates a second story between the lines; the reader becomes an investigator of the narration itself.
narrator_reliability_types.caution: The text must supply the correcting evidence, or unreliability is indistinguishable from an authorial mistake.

narrator_reliability_types.name: misreporting
narrator_reliability_types.definition: Unreliability along the axis of facts: the narrator states events wrongly.
narrator_reliability_types.example: He says the meeting was on a Thursday; two documents in the same chapter date it to Monday.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: The most detectable unreliability, because it can be contradicted by evidence in the text.

narrator_reliability_types.name: misreading
narrator_reliability_types.definition: Unreliability along the axis of interpretation: the narrator reports accurately but understands wrongly.
narrator_reliability_types.example: He reports that she left the room without a word and concludes she agreed.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: The reader sees past the narrator using the narrator's own data; produces dramatic irony.

narrator_reliability_types.name: misevaluating
narrator_reliability_types.definition: Unreliability along the axis of ethics or value: the narrator's judgment of what happened is one the text repudiates.
narrator_reliability_types.example: He calls the reclassification 'housekeeping' and expects the reader to agree that nobody was harmed.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: Puts the reader's moral sense in tension with the narrating voice.

narrator_reliability_types.name: underreporting
narrator_reliability_types.definition: Unreliability by omission: the narrator knows more than they say.
narrator_reliability_types.example: The account of that March covers eleven pages and never mentions where he was on the fourteenth.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: Creates suspicion from absence; readers notice a shape-shaped hole.
narrator_reliability_types.caution: The omission must be conspicuous, or it reads as the author forgetting.

narrator_reliability_types.name: underreading
narrator_reliability_types.definition: Unreliability by insufficient interpretation: the narrator perceives correctly but does not draw the inference the reader draws.
narrator_reliability_types.example: The child narrator records that the adults stopped talking whenever she came into the kitchen, and thinks it is about her birthday.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: The engine of naive narration; poignancy comes from the gap.

narrator_reliability_types.name: underregarding
narrator_reliability_types.definition: Unreliability by insufficient ethical response: the narrator judges in the right direction but far too weakly.
narrator_reliability_types.example: He describes the town's collapse and calls it, twice, 'unfortunate'.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: Characterizes the narrator's moral scale without any explicit condemnation.

narrator_reliability_types.name: bonding unreliability
narrator_reliability_types.definition: Unreliability that draws the reader closer to the narrator — the gap between their views is one the reader forgives or shares.
narrator_reliability_types.example: Her self-deprecation about the audit is plainly excessive, and it makes the reader like her more.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: Intimacy through the flaw; the reader is on the narrator's side against the narrator's own account.

narrator_reliability_types.name: estranging unreliability
narrator_reliability_types.definition: Unreliability that pushes the reader away, widening the distance between reader and narrator.
narrator_reliability_types.example: His explanation of why the clerk deserved to be fired is coherent, detailed, and appalling.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: The reader watches the narrator from outside and begins reading against him.

narrator_reliability_types.name: naive narrator
narrator_reliability_types.definition: A narrator whose limited experience or understanding prevents them from grasping what they accurately report.
narrator_reliability_types.example: A new clerk describes the missing March pages as a filing problem someone will get around to.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: The reader supplies the meaning; every innocent sentence carries a second reading.
narrator_reliability_types.caution: The narrator must remain plausibly limited — sudden insight breaks the whole arrangement.

narrator_reliability_types.name: self-deceived narrator
narrator_reliability_types.definition: A narrator who has an interest in not knowing what they know, and whose account is shaped by that interest.
narrator_reliability_types.example: He describes the folder as one he never opened, in a paragraph that reports what page three said.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: Unreliability without lying; the contradictions are between sentences, not against the world.

narrator_reliability_types.name: deceptive narrator
narrator_reliability_types.definition: A narrator who knowingly lies to the reader.
narrator_reliability_types.example: The account of the night the boxes moved is complete, confident, and later shown to be an invention.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: Turns the reading experience retroactively into a puzzle; the reveal recasts everything.
narrator_reliability_types.caution: The text must have played fair — the evidence for the lie has to be present before the reveal.

narrator_reliability_types.name: fallible narrator
narrator_reliability_types.definition: A narrator who is honest and mistaken: limited access, faulty memory, ordinary error, no intent to mislead.
narrator_reliability_types.example: She remembers the drive as taking an hour; the toll receipt in the same chapter says twenty minutes.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: Realism rather than trickery; memoirs are fallible by nature.

narrator_reliability_types.name: partial-knowledge narrator
narrator_reliability_types.definition: A narrator whose account is limited by structural lack of access rather than by any personal failing.
narrator_reliability_types.example: The clerk can report everything that crossed her desk and nothing that was discussed upstairs.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: Reliability inside a boundary; the boundary itself becomes a plot constraint.
narrator_reliability_types.caution: Establish the boundary early or readers will read the gaps as evasion.

narrator_reliability_types.name: self-justifying narrator
narrator_reliability_types.definition: A narrator whose telling is organized as a defense, addressed implicitly or explicitly to a judge.
narrator_reliability_types.example: Everything in the account is arranged around the sentence 'anyone would have done the same', which the account never states.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: Every detail selected becomes evidence of the selection; the reader reads for what the defense omits.

narrator_reliability_types.name: corroborating detail
narrator_reliability_types.definition: A technique rather than a narrator type: planting independently verifiable details so the reader can measure the narrator against them.
narrator_reliability_types.example: The narrator's dates are checkable against a chapter epigraph drawn from the docket.
narrator_reliability_types.effect: Gives the reader an instrument; without one, unreliability is unrecoverable.
narrator_reliability_types.caution: Plant at least two before the reveal, or the twist will read as arbitrary.

narrative_voice_textures.name: plain style
narrative_voice_textures.definition: A voice built from short common words, transparent syntax, and few figures, aiming at unnoticeable clarity.
narrative_voice_textures.example: The plant closed in March. Twelve hundred people worked there. Most of them heard about it on the radio.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: Reads as honest and unmediated; puts the material forward and the writer behind it.
narrative_voice_textures.caution: Plainness is a rhetorical position, not the absence of one — it claims a truthfulness it must earn.

narrative_voice_textures.name: ornate style
narrative_voice_textures.definition: A voice of long periodic sentences, Latinate diction, and elaborated figures.
narrative_voice_textures.example: It was the peculiar genius of the arrangement that no participant in it could be shown, on any single day, to have done anything whatever.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: Signals intellectual formality and confidence; makes complexity feel governed.
narrative_voice_textures.caution: Ornate prose that is not thinking hard reads as bluster.

narrative_voice_textures.name: ironic voice
narrative_voice_textures.definition: A narration whose stated evaluations differ predictably from the ones the text endorses.
narrative_voice_textures.example: The board handled the matter with the seriousness that four separate lunches can convey.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: Lets the writer criticize without asserting, and flatters readers who catch it.
narrative_voice_textures.caution: Sustained irony leaves nowhere to stand when the material turns genuinely grave.

narrative_voice_textures.name: deadpan
narrative_voice_textures.definition: Flat, unmodulated delivery of material that would ordinarily be inflected.
narrative_voice_textures.example: The building had been condemned twice and was, at the time of the hearing, hosting the hearing.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: The absence of comment is the comment; the reader supplies the outrage or the laugh.

narrative_voice_textures.name: elegiac voice
narrative_voice_textures.definition: A voice organized around loss, tending toward the past habitual, the long cadence, and the naming of vanished particulars.
narrative_voice_textures.example: There had been a diner across from the gate, and a shift-change so regular the traffic light was timed to it.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: Mourns without stating grief; the accumulation of detail does the work.
narrative_voice_textures.caution: Nostalgia is the failure mode — specificity is what separates elegy from sentiment.

narrative_voice_textures.name: urgent voice
narrative_voice_textures.definition: Short sentences, present tense or clipped past, minimal subordination, high verb density.
narrative_voice_textures.example: She takes the stairs. Two flights. The door at the bottom is chained.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: Compresses reading time toward event time; readers speed up because the syntax lets them.
narrative_voice_textures.caution: Uniform urgency reads as monotony; it needs a slow passage to press against.

narrative_voice_textures.name: clinical voice
narrative_voice_textures.definition: Precise, unemotional narration using technical or procedural vocabulary about emotionally charged material.
narrative_voice_textures.example: The reclassification moved eleven million dollars from a restricted line to an unrestricted one. Nothing else about the account changed.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: Restraint amplifies: the reader supplies the feeling the prose refuses.

narrative_voice_textures.name: vernacular voice
narrative_voice_textures.definition: Narration in a regional or social idiom, with its syntax, idioms, and rhythms carried into the narration itself.
narrative_voice_textures.example: Nobody around here ever called it a bank failure. They called it the year the Hendricks boys got quiet.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: Locates the telling in a community; the narrator becomes a member rather than an observer.
narrative_voice_textures.caution: Must be sustained consistently; a vernacular that lapses reads as condescension.

narrative_voice_textures.name: confiding voice
narrative_voice_textures.definition: A narrator who addresses the reader as a trusted intimate, admitting uncertainty and sharing asides.
narrative_voice_textures.example: I should say here that I liked him, which is probably why it took me two years to check anything he told me.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: Builds trust through admitted fallibility; the reader is a confidant rather than an audience.

narrative_voice_textures.name: oracular voice
narrative_voice_textures.definition: Elevated, declarative narration that pronounces rather than argues, often in the present tense and with parallel constructions.
narrative_voice_textures.example: Institutions do not fall. They are hollowed, and then one day someone leans on them.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: Confers authority; readers feel addressed from above the story.
narrative_voice_textures.caution: Every oracular sentence is an unsupported claim wearing a robe; ration them.

narrative_voice_textures.name: hard-boiled voice
narrative_voice_textures.definition: First-person narration in clipped declaratives, concrete nouns, and understated wit, withholding emotion.
narrative_voice_textures.example: The office had two chairs and one of them was for people who were leaving.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: Characterizes the narrator through what he declines to say; the style is the psychology.
narrative_voice_textures.caution: Now heavily codified; a single wrong flourish tips it into pastiche.

narrative_voice_textures.name: lyrical voice
narrative_voice_textures.definition: Narration foregrounding sound, image, and cadence, with attention to rhythm at the phrase level.
narrative_voice_textures.example: The river came up through the floorboards the way light does, slowly and then all at once and then everywhere.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: Slows reading and makes the prose itself an object of attention.
narrative_voice_textures.caution: Lyricism competes with information; use where the reader needs to feel rather than follow.

narrative_voice_textures.name: comic hyperbolic voice
narrative_voice_textures.definition: Narration that escalates its terms past proportion for comic effect.
narrative_voice_textures.example: The agenda ran to nine items, of which four were the same item and one was lunch.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: The exaggeration signals the narrator's exasperation without stating it.
narrative_voice_textures.caution: Hyperbole spends credibility; a narrator who exaggerates about small things will not be believed about large ones.

narrative_voice_textures.name: bureaucratic pastiche
narrative_voice_textures.definition: Narration adopting institutional language — passive constructions, nominalizations, procedural euphemism — as a satirical or characterizing device.
narrative_voice_textures.example: A determination was made that further escalation would not be productive at that time.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: Reproduces the machine's own voice, which condemns it more efficiently than commentary.
narrative_voice_textures.caution: It is deliberately bad prose; keep the passages short and clearly framed.

narrative_voice_textures.name: incantatory voice
narrative_voice_textures.definition: Narration built on repetition, parallelism, and accumulating rhythm.
narrative_voice_textures.example: They asked in March. They asked in June. They asked in writing, and in person, and through a lawyer, and in March again.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: Produces the pressure of ritual; repetition converts a list into an accusation.
narrative_voice_textures.caution: Powerful and quickly exhausted; one passage per chapter at most.

narrative_voice_textures.name: aphoristic voice
narrative_voice_textures.definition: Narration that periodically compresses its argument into a short, balanced, generalizable sentence.
narrative_voice_textures.example: Money never disappears. It only changes the name of the line it sits on.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: Gives the reader portable formulations; strongly associated with authority.
narrative_voice_textures.caution: Aphorism sounds true whether or not it is; each one should be defensible as a claim.

narrative_voice_textures.name: reticent voice
narrative_voice_textures.definition: A narrator who visibly declines to say things — refusing interpretation, skipping over the obvious climax, stating less than is known.
narrative_voice_textures.example: What happened in the parking lot afterward is not something I am going to set down here.
narrative_voice_textures.effect: The withholding characterizes the narrator and charges the omitted material.
narrative_voice_textures.caution: Readers tolerate one or two refusals; more and they suspect the writer of having nothing to withhold.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: we-of-shared-discovery
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: A first-person plural that enlists the reader as co-investigator, moving through evidence together with the writer.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: If we line the two statements up by date, we find that one of them describes a reserve the other has already spent.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Converts exposition into shared reasoning; conclusions feel derived rather than delivered.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: The false 'we' — assuming agreement the reader has not given — is the mode's characteristic dishonesty.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: direct address
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: The writer speaks to the reader as 'you', naming their likely reaction, question, or objection.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: You are going to want to know why nobody simply asked. So did I.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Anticipates and disarms resistance; keeps the reader present in an argument.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: Telling readers what they think is a bet; when it misses, they disengage.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: authorial intrusion
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: The writer steps out of the material to comment on it, on the process, or on themselves.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: I have read this paragraph of the minutes perhaps forty times and I still cannot make it mean anything else.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Reveals the human doing the work, which can raise or lower credibility depending on how it is used.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: Each intrusion must add something the reader could not supply; otherwise it is throat-clearing.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: reconstructed scene
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: A dramatized scene built from documents, interviews, and record, narrated with fictional technique but no invented fact.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: At 9:40 the deputy carried the box down to the annex — the log records the time, and two people remember the box.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Gives nonfiction the immediacy of narrative while keeping every element sourced.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: Every detail needs a source, and the sourcing convention should be stated somewhere the reader can find it.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: immersion reportage
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: First-person narration by a writer who has entered the world being described and reports from inside it.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: I spent four months on the second floor of that annex, and by the end the clerks had stopped explaining things to me.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: The writer's access and change become part of the evidence.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: The reporter's experience can crowd out the subject's; keep asking whose story this is.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: fly-on-the-wall reportage
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: Third-person narration of observed events with the reporter's presence suppressed.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: The three of them sat in the conference room for forty minutes without opening the folder on the table.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Gives observed material the authority of unmediated fact.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: The suppression is a choice; if the reporter's presence changed the scene, hiding it is a distortion.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: expository first person
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: A functional 'I' used to state method, position, and limits without narrating the writer's experience.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: I use 'reclassification' throughout in the narrow sense the examiners used, not the accounting one.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Makes the writer's choices visible and auditable without making them the subject.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: provisional essayistic I
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: A first person that thinks in public, advancing and revising positions as the essay proceeds.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: I want to say the failure was structural. But I have just written three pages of names, and structures do not sign things.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Enacts inquiry rather than reporting its conclusion; the essay's founding move.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: The revision must be real; staged reconsideration is transparent.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: case-study narration
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: A single instance narrated in detail as an instrument for a general claim.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: One county, one bank, one filing cabinet: what happened here happened, with different names, in eleven other places that year.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Grounds abstraction in a followable story while explicitly marking its representative status.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: State the basis for representativeness, or the case becomes an anecdote pretending to be evidence.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: second-person instructional
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: Procedural narration addressed to the reader as the actor.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: You start with the index, not the documents, because the index tells you what was removed.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Puts the reader in the role of practitioner; the clearest mode for method.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: imperative mode
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: Direct commands with the subject suppressed.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: Pull the index first. Photograph every page before anyone joins you.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Fastest possible instruction; each sentence is an action.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: Unbroken imperatives read as hectoring; alternate with explanation of why.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: thought experiment
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: Narration of a hypothetical scenario invited on the reader's own terms.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: Suppose you are the only person in the building who has seen both statements, and suppose the person you report to signed one of them.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Lets a reader test a principle without committing to a factual claim.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: Mark clearly where the hypothetical ends; readers carry invented details into the factual passages.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: omniscient historian
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: Third-person narration of past events with access to outcomes, motives, and multiple vantages, grounded in the record.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: Neither man knew that the schedule they were arguing about had already been filed under the following year.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: The historian's version of omniscience: hindsight and archive standing in for access to minds.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: Attributing interior states requires a source; 'he felt' needs a diary or an interview behind it.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: quote-weaving
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: Building narration around interview or document quotations, the writer's sentences supplying frame and connective logic.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: She calls it "a paperwork thing." The examiner's report uses the word "concealment" nine times.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Lets sources speak while the writer's arrangement carries the argument.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: Arrangement is argument; juxtaposing two quotations makes a claim you are responsible for.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: method disclosure
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: Narration that shows the seams — how the material was obtained, what was refused, what remains unknown.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: The bank declined to comment. Two former directors spoke on condition that their departments not be named.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Credibility through visible limits; readers trust an account that maps its own edges.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: Method that becomes the story is a common failure of investigative narrative.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: retrospective self-correction
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: The writer revisits and revises something asserted earlier in the same work.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: Earlier I called this an accounting error. Having now read the March correspondence, I would not use that phrase.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Models intellectual honesty and lets the reader watch a conclusion form.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: Only works if the earlier claim was made in good faith; retroactive staging is detectable.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: institutional voice
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: An impersonal, unattributed 'we' or agentless third person speaking for an organization or publication.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: This newspaper has sought the schedule for eleven months.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Confers institutional rather than personal authority.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: It also diffuses responsibility; readers increasingly hear the diffusion.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: composite scene
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: A scene assembled from several real occasions and presented as one.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: A typical Friday at the annex, drawn from three visits and presented as one afternoon.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Achieves narrative economy at the cost of literal accuracy.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: Never present a composite as a specific occasion without disclosing it; in most nonfiction contracts this is simply not permitted.

nonfiction_narration_modes.name: data narration
nonfiction_narration_modes.definition: Narration that walks the reader through a quantity's behavior over time as if it were a character with a trajectory.
nonfiction_narration_modes.example: The reserve line holds flat for six years, jumps in a single March, and then never appears again.
nonfiction_narration_modes.effect: Gives numbers a shape and a story arc without a chart.
nonfiction_narration_modes.caution: Anthropomorphized data can smuggle in causal claims the numbers do not support.

temporal_manipulation.name: analepsis
temporal_manipulation.definition: Narration of an event earlier than the point the main narrative has reached.
temporal_manipulation.example: Before the hearing there had been a Sunday in March that nobody had thought worth mentioning.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Supplies cause after consequence, so the reader learns why with the stakes already established.
temporal_manipulation.caution: Every flashback stops forward motion; it must return the reader with something they now need.

temporal_manipulation.name: external analepsis
temporal_manipulation.definition: A flashback to a time before the main narrative's starting point.
temporal_manipulation.example: The annex had been built in 1932 for exactly this purpose, which is a story of its own.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Supplies deep background without extending the main timeline.
temporal_manipulation.caution: External analepses read as digression unless they are tied explicitly to the present question.

temporal_manipulation.name: internal analepsis
temporal_manipulation.definition: A flashback to a moment inside the main narrative's span that was skipped or withheld.
temporal_manipulation.example: We can now return to the Thursday the box was signed out, which this account passed over the first time.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Fills a gap the reader has already noticed; the standard mechanism of a reveal.

temporal_manipulation.name: prolepsis
temporal_manipulation.definition: Narratological sense (Genette): narration of an event later than the point the main narrative has reached.
temporal_manipulation.example: The clerk who filed it would testify about that afternoon four years later, and would not be believed.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Trades suspense of outcome for suspense of process; the reader now watches how rather than whether.
temporal_manipulation.caution: Each prolepsis spends the outcome; keep an accounting of what the reader already knows.

temporal_manipulation.name: narratorial foreshadowing
temporal_manipulation.definition: A retrospective narrator's brief signal of a future consequence without narrating the future scene.
temporal_manipulation.example: I would remember the exact wording of that sentence for a long time.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Raises tension cheaply and marks a detail as load-bearing.
temporal_manipulation.caution: The most abused device in first-person retrospective narration; two per chapter is already many.

temporal_manipulation.name: summary
temporal_manipulation.definition: Duration sense (Genette): narration in which story time exceeds discourse time — years or weeks compressed into sentences. Distinct from the RST summary relation, which is a restatement move.
temporal_manipulation.example: For the next three years the file moved between two offices and nobody read it.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Covers ground; controls how much of a life the reader has to sit through.
temporal_manipulation.caution: Sustained summary flattens; readers need scene to attach to.

temporal_manipulation.name: scene
temporal_manipulation.definition: Narration in which discourse time approximates story time — dialogue and action rendered moment by moment.
temporal_manipulation.example: "Where is the schedule?" "With the auditors." "Which auditors?" He did not answer.
temporal_manipulation.effect: The reader experiences events rather than being told about them; the default unit of dramatic writing.

temporal_manipulation.name: descriptive pause
temporal_manipulation.definition: Narration in which story time stops while discourse continues — description, background, or commentary.
temporal_manipulation.example: The annex was two rooms and a corridor, lit by one window at the far end, with cabinets to the ceiling.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Holds the story still to let the reader see; also a way to build dread before an event resumes.
temporal_manipulation.caution: Pauses placed at moments of high tension read as authorial teasing.

temporal_manipulation.name: stretch
temporal_manipulation.definition: Narration in which discourse time exceeds story time — a few seconds rendered across many sentences.
temporal_manipulation.example: The drawer came open four inches. She could see the top of a folder, the corner of a second one behind it, and then the drawer stopped.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Slow motion; the expansion signals that these seconds matter.
temporal_manipulation.caution: Only for genuine turning points; elsewhere it reads as padding.

temporal_manipulation.name: temporal ellipsis
temporal_manipulation.definition: An unnarrated gap: story time passes with no discourse at all.
temporal_manipulation.example: White space, and then: 'By the time the report was public, both of them had left the state.'
temporal_manipulation.effect: Skips what does not need telling, and can conceal something the reader will demand later.
temporal_manipulation.caution: A concealing ellipsis is a promise; readers will notice a gap around the crucial event.

temporal_manipulation.name: singulative narration
temporal_manipulation.definition: Telling once what happened once — the default frequency.
temporal_manipulation.example: On the fourteenth she drove to the annex and signed the box out.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Marks an occasion as particular rather than typical.

temporal_manipulation.name: iterative narration
temporal_manipulation.definition: Telling once what happened repeatedly.
temporal_manipulation.example: Every Friday she signed a box out, and every Monday she signed it back.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Establishes routine efficiently, so that a single deviation from it can carry enormous weight.
temporal_manipulation.caution: Iterative passages have no tension of their own; keep them short and use them to set up a break.

temporal_manipulation.name: repeating narration
temporal_manipulation.definition: Telling more than once what happened once, often from different vantages or in different words.
temporal_manipulation.example: The afternoon is narrated three times: as the deputy remembers it, as the log records it, and as the hearing reconstructed it.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Makes the act of telling visible and turns discrepancy into the subject.
temporal_manipulation.caution: Each retelling must add or contradict; identical repetition merely costs pages.

temporal_manipulation.name: anachrony
temporal_manipulation.definition: Any discrepancy between the order of events and the order of their narration.
temporal_manipulation.example: The book opens with the hearing, moves back nine years, and reaches the hearing again in its last chapter.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Lets the writer sequence for meaning rather than chronology.
temporal_manipulation.caution: Every anachrony taxes the reader's timeline-building; give them anchors.

temporal_manipulation.name: achrony
temporal_manipulation.definition: Narration of events whose position in the timeline is never established.
temporal_manipulation.example: An undated memo appears between chapters, and the book never says when it was written.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Produces unease and, in mystery, a piece the reader cannot yet place.
temporal_manipulation.caution: Unresolved achrony reads as an oversight unless the text signals that the date is unavailable.

temporal_manipulation.name: reverse chronology
temporal_manipulation.definition: Narration proceeding backward, each section preceding the one before it.
temporal_manipulation.example: The last chapter is the first signature; the first chapter is the bankruptcy.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Replaces 'what happens' with 'how did this become inevitable'; every scene is read as cause.
temporal_manipulation.caution: Demands very clear signposting; readers lose the sequence quickly.

temporal_manipulation.name: braided timelines
temporal_manipulation.definition: Two or more chronologies alternated by section, converging or commenting on each other.
temporal_manipulation.example: Odd chapters follow the 1978 audit; even chapters follow the 2003 lawsuit that reopened it.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Puts cause and consequence in dialogue and lets each strand solve the other's exposition problem.
temporal_manipulation.caution: The strands must progress at comparable rates or readers will start skipping one.

temporal_manipulation.name: simultaneity
temporal_manipulation.definition: Narration marking that two lines of action occupy the same time.
temporal_manipulation.pattern: Meanwhile / At the same hour / While [clause]
temporal_manipulation.example: While the committee argued about the agenda, two floors down the boxes were going out to a truck.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Creates dramatic irony and lets the reader hold more than any character can.
temporal_manipulation.caution: 'Meanwhile' is the crudest available signal; a time stamp or a repeated detail usually works better.

temporal_manipulation.name: time stamp
temporal_manipulation.definition: An explicit date, time, or dateline marking a section's position in the chronology.
temporal_manipulation.example: March 14, 9:40 a.m. The deputy signs the log.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Removes all navigational ambiguity, which is why complex nonfiction chronologies rely on it.

temporal_manipulation.name: montage compression
temporal_manipulation.definition: A rapid series of brief images or fragments standing in for an extended period.
temporal_manipulation.example: Two more audits. A new letterhead. The annex window boarded from the inside. Nobody in the building who remembered March.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Passes time while keeping sensory texture, where summary would go abstract.
temporal_manipulation.caution: Fragments must be concrete; abstract montage is just a list of nouns.

temporal_manipulation.name: memory trigger
temporal_manipulation.definition: A present-moment sensory detail that motivates a shift into an earlier time.
temporal_manipulation.example: The smell of floor wax in the stairwell, and it was 1978 again.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Naturalizes a flashback so the reader experiences it as association rather than authorial arrangement.
temporal_manipulation.caution: The most conventionalized transition in narrative prose; vary the mechanism across a book.

temporal_manipulation.name: narrative present as pivot
temporal_manipulation.definition: A recurring 'now' — a scene, a room, a moment — that the narrative repeatedly returns to between excursions in time.
temporal_manipulation.example: Every chapter returns to the hearing room and the unopened box on the table before departing again.
temporal_manipulation.effect: Gives an anachronic structure a fixed point, so the reader always knows where home is.
